rationale: Switch from the referential montage to the clinical neonatal bipolar double-banana (18 derivations). Each recording is first band-pass filtered to 0.5–30 Hz and downsampled to 64 Hz. With a shared reference, a focal low-amplitude seizure is mixed into every channel along with reference and drift artifacts. Bipolar derivations localise it to neighbouring electrodes, which should make the per-channel max features pick up seizures much better. The filtering also removes DC drift and high-frequency EMG/line noise.

The neonatal EEG background varies a lot between babies (amplitude, maturity, electrode impedance), so absolute log line length and band powers mean different things in different recordings. I'm adding a robust per-recording normalised copy of every feature: subtract the recording's median and divide by its IQR. The classifier can then see "unusually rhythmic or energetic for this baby" as well as absolute level. This is label-free and done per item inside `featurize`.

The current features only measure amplitude and band power, which are driven as much by artifacts and differences in background between babies as by seizures. Neonatal seizures are rhythmic discharges, so I'm adding three rhythmicity measures for each channel and taking their max and median across channels: the autocorrelation peak after the first zero crossing in the 0.5–15 Hz band, the fraction of power at the dominant spectral peak, and negative spectral entropy. These give the classifier a direct measure of periodicity that does not depend on amplitude.

Right now each second is classified from one 8 s window, but neonatal seizures last tens of seconds to minutes and evolve. A sustained rise in rhythmicity or line length over ~15–60 s separates them from brief artifacts or isolated sharp waves. So I'm adding multi-scale temporal context: for each recording, I compute the centered rolling means of all 18 features over 15 s and 61 s windows and their rolling max over 15 s. This is label-free and done per recording.

Rows within one neonate are strongly autocorrelated, and the rolling-context features make neighbouring seconds almost identical. So the default GBM (leaves of 20 samples, 31 leaves, learning rate 0.1) can fit neonate-specific few-second patterns rather than seizure patterns that generalise across neonates. I'm changing only the GBM settings: smaller trees, leaves of at least 1000 samples (several minutes of EEG, so a leaf can't rest on one brief event), L2 penalty, and a lower learning rate with more iterations. This should give smoother decision functions that rank seconds consistently across neonates, which is what concatenated AUROC measures. The values are a single fixed choice, not tuned with inner CV.

I'm adding the clinical neonatal double-banana bipolar montage alongside the referential one, not replacing it as round 1 did. Each 8 s window's 18 bipolar derivations are built on the fly as electrode differences, with no filter or resampling changes, and the same 9 per-channel features are aggregated (max/median) separately for each montage. Neonatal seizures are focal, so bipolar derivations localise them, and they cancel common-mode rhythmic artifacts such as ECG and reference contamination. Those artifacts currently inflate the referential rhythmicity and power maxima. The referential features stay available for broadly distributed seizures.

The current features cannot tell seizures apart from rhythmic or high-energy artifacts that are common in NICU recordings: EMG, movement or respiration drift, and ECG or reference contamination. So far each second gets just one feature set, so a neonate without seizures but with artifacts produces confident false positives across the whole recording, which hurts concatenated AUROC. I'm adding artifact-sensitive descriptors for each channel: log relative EMG-band power (30–48 Hz, below the 50 Hz mains line) and log relative very-low-frequency drift power (<0.5 Hz), each aggregated as max and median over channels. I'm also adding one global feature, the mean inter-channel correlation of the 0.5–30 Hz signal. That correlation is high for common-mode artifacts such as ECG and reference contamination and low for focal seizures. All of these go through the same rolling-context and GBM pipeline as the existing features.

Smoothing is currently fixed at 10 s, yet Helsinki seizures typically run from tens of seconds to minutes, and concatenated AUROC suffers from short isolated false-positive bursts. I'm keeping the features and GBM unchanged and choosing the width of the moving-average output smoother (1–120 s) with a 3-fold inner grouped CV on each training fold, scored by concatenated AUROC on out-of-fold predictions. The harness score is never used for this choice.

I'm adding local-background contrast features: the 15 s rolling mean of each base feature minus that feature's rolling median over the surrounding 10 minutes. A seizure is an evolving change from the baby's own background, and a 10-minute median stays near background unless a seizure takes up most of the window. This compares each baby to its own background without discarding the absolute levels, which is where global per-recording normalization went wrong in round 2. It also hands the GBM differences that additive trees struggle to build from separate columns.

At the moment the max over channels is taken each second and only then averaged over time, so the max can hop from channel to channel and transient artifacts on different electrodes look as strong as a seizure. A focal neonatal seizure, by contrast, stays rhythmic and energetic on the same channel for tens of seconds. I'm adding channel-consistent context features: each channel's own 15 s rolling mean, and that mean minus the channel's own 10-minute background median, each maxed over channels. This should pick up sustained focal discharges and discount a single bad electrode that is always high.

Right now the only post-processing is one moving-average width picked by inner CV. This change replaces it with a learned second stage: a heavily regularized GBM trained on the multi-scale temporal context of the stage-1 out-of-fold logits. Its inputs are moving means over 5–121 s, 15 s and 61 s maxima, and the 15 s mean minus the 10-minute background median of the stage-1 output. Neonatal seizures build up over tens of seconds and stand out from that neonate's own baseline, so the second stage can learn something like hysteresis and background-relative scoring, and it can still reproduce the old smoother.

I'm adding the third-largest channel value for the two channel-consistent features: each channel's 15 s mean, and that mean minus the channel's own 10-minute background. The current feature takes only the max across channels, so one bad electrode or a single-electrode pop looks just as strong as a seizure. A real neonatal seizure lasts tens of seconds and involves a group of neighbouring electrodes, especially in this referential montage, so it should push at least 3 channels above their own background together.

I'm adding Hjorth mobility and complexity for each channel, computed on the 0.5–30 Hz band-limited window. These are time-domain measures of mean frequency and of how close the waveform is to a sinusoid. Rhythmic neonatal discharges are nearly sinusoidal, giving low complexity, while EMG, spikes and broadband artifacts give high complexity. Because the measures come from the waveform rather than the spectral peak, they should still capture rhythmicity when the discharge frequency drifts inside the 8 s window. Both go through the same max/median, temporal-context, background-contrast and channel-consistent aggregation as the other features.

I'm adding per-channel persistence of the dominant frequency: a neonatal seizure keeps a stable, slowly drifting discharge frequency on the same electrodes for tens of seconds, while the background's spectral peak jumps around at random. For each channel I find the dominant 0.5–8 Hz frequency on a 1/f²-whitened spectrum, so the 1/f background doesn't always lock onto the lowest bin. I then take its rolling 21 s standard deviation (log2 Hz) and keep the minimum, 3rd-smallest and median across channels, plus each of those minus its 10-minute background median.

Blend the regularized GBM with an L2 logistic regression trained on the same clipped, standardized features. Blending is done in logit space, and the inner grouped CV picks the blend weight together with the smoothing width (weight 0 keeps the GBM alone). Trees with large leaves give step-shaped, saturating scores that rank seconds poorly across neonates they have not seen, whereas a linear model on the background-contrast and rhythmicity features extrapolates smoothly, so its ranking errors should partly cancel the GBM's on concatenated AUROC.

Concatenated AUROC is hurt by baby-specific offsets in the model output, such as a seizure-free neonate whose artifacts keep its whole recording at an elevated score. So after smoothing I subtract alpha times a low quantile of each recording's own logits, which is a label-free per-neonate baseline correction. The inner grouped CV picks alpha (0 keeps the current behaviour) and the quantile together with the smoothing width.

Channel-consistent context gave the biggest recent gains (rounds 10 and 12), but it only looks at a 15 s window, while Helsinki seizures typically last from about one to several minutes. A real focal seizure stays on the same electrodes for that long, whereas artifacts on any one channel are short. I'm adding a 61 s version of the same features: each channel's own 61 s rolling mean minus that channel's own 10-minute background. I take its max and its 3rd-largest value over channels, so sustained regional activity is separated from short single-channel bursts.

The current spatial-spread features take the max and the 3rd-largest value across all electrodes, wherever they are on the scalp. A neonatal seizure is focal, though: it involves one electrode and its immediate scalp neighbours, while artifacts on scattered single electrodes do not. So I'm adding a montage-aware regional aggregation. Each channel's 15 s and 61 s background contrasts are averaged with those of its adjacent 10-20 electrodes, and the max over channels of each regional average is taken. This should pick out sustained, contiguous regional discharges that the global top-k can't tell apart from coincidences on non-adjacent electrodes.

Some Helsinki neonates have a high seizure burden, with seizures lasting many minutes up to status epilepticus. In those recordings the per-channel 10-minute rolling median is itself mostly seizure, so the existing background-contrast features fall to zero just where the seizure burden is highest. This change adds one contrast that holds up when seizures dominate. It takes each channel's 61 s mean, subtracts that channel's rolling 30-minute 20th percentile (a long, low-quantile reference that stays at the non-seizure level even when most of the window is seizure), and summarises the result as the max, the 3rd-largest and the scalp-neighbourhood max over channels.

All channel features are currently aggregated across channels one feature at a time, so the maximum rhythmicity can come from one electrode and the maximum power from another. A seizure is the same electrodes becoming rhythmic and energetic at once, while artifacts usually raise only one of the two. This round adds per-channel conjunction features. Each channel's 15 s, 61 s and 30-min low-quantile background contrasts are put on a common scale by their within-recording robust spread (label-free). Two composites are built per channel: min(mean rhythmicity z, mean power/line-length z), which is high only when both rise together, and a mean over the nine seizure-related z-scores. Each composite is then summarised as the max, the 3rd-largest and the scalp-neighbourhood max over channels.
